# Exact obstruction to the unrestricted finite-base gamma_d/h(P) target

The proposed stronger target for **arbitrary finite base sets** is FALSE.
This is not an OC counterexample. The three-site sampling set below is
not a complete lattice intersection, and converting its coordinates to
integers creates many additional integer fibers of positive volume.

All data below are rational. No limiting argument or numerical
optimization is used. The exact maximum depth is calculated.

## 1. A positive actual three-fiber convex family

Use d=2 and one real base coordinate z. Let

    P={0,t,1}, t=1/100,
    A=[1/100,27/100] x [1/100,26/100],
    B={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=1},
    D={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=21/20}.

Put A at base0, B at base t, and D at base1. Their areas are

    a=13/200, b=1/2, c=441/800,
    M=a+b+c=893/800.                                (1)

Let C be the convex hull of these three fibers. It is a compact convex
body with nonempty interior in R^3. The endpoint sections are exactly
A and D. The middle section is exactly B because

    (1-t)A+tD subset int(B).                         (2)

Indeed both coordinates in this Minkowski combination are at least
(1-t)/100>0, and its coordinate sum is at most

    (99/100)(53/100)+(1/100)(21/20)
      =669/1250<1.

Every convex combination contributing to the t-section either comes
from B or is a convex combination of a point of B and a point of
(1-t)A+tD. More explicitly, if the endpoint coefficients are alpha
and delta and the coefficient of B is eta, the base equation gives
delta=t(1-eta), alpha=(1-t)(1-eta). Thus (2) proves that the entire
actual t-section is B. All three measured fibers are full-dimensional.

Their finite-base Helly number is h(P)=2. Any convex trace on the line
is an interval trace on the three ordered points. For a finite family
of nonempty such traces, the trace with largest lower endpoint and
the trace with smallest upper endpoint determine whether their common
intersection is empty; two traces therefore suffice. An empty trace
already suffices alone. Two disjoint singleton traces show h(P)>=2.

## 2. Three explicit caps covering the whole middle plane

Write Q=49/200. Consider the following closed ambient halfspaces:

    H_0={-x-y-2(z-t)>=-3/5},
    H_1={ x   -2(z-t)>= 3/10},
    H_2={ y   -2(z-t)>= 3/10}.                       (3)

They cover the entire plane z=t: the three left-minus-right margins
sum to zero there, so they cannot all be negative at any point.

At base0, H_0 contains all of A, because its coordinate sum is at
most53/100<3/5+2/100. H_1 and H_2 miss all of A, because their
threshold at this base is 3/10-2/100=7/25, which is greater than
27/100 and26/100 respectively.

At base1, every cap in (3) misses D. The first would require
-x-y>=-3/5+198/100=69/50>0. The other two would require the
corresponding coordinate to be at least3/10+198/100=57/25,
greater than21/20.

At base t, the B-cap areas are respectively

    (3/5)^2/2=9/50,
    (1-3/10)^2/2=49/200,
    (1-3/10)^2/2=49/200.

Consequently each cap in (3) has exactly the same total measured mass:

    mu(H_0)=9/50+13/200=Q,
    mu(H_1)=mu(H_2)=Q.                              (4)

Thus every candidate in the middle fiber has depth at most Q/M.
The integer and continuous normal coefficients are retained: these
are actual oblique ambient caps, not merely cuts inside B.

## 3. Explicit endpoint-plane covers

At base0, the two caps

    {x-100 z>=7/50},
    {-x-100 z>=-7/50}                              (5)

cover its entire plane and divide A into its equal-area vertical halves.
They exclude both B and D. At z=t, for example, the maximum left side
of the first is1-1=0<7/50, and the maximum left side of the second is
0-1=-1<-7/50. At z=1 the exclusions are even stronger. Hence each
cap in (5) has mass a/2=13/400<Q.

At base1, the three caps

    {-x-y+2(z-1)>=-7/10},
    { x  +2(z-1)>= 7/20},
    { y  +2(z-1)>= 7/20}                            (6)

cover its whole plane. The margins again sum to zero there. All three
exclude A and B: at z=t the maximum left sides are -198/100 for the
first and1-198/100 for each of the other two, strictly below their
thresholds; the values at z=0 are smaller still. In D these are its
three centroid vertex caps. Their areas are all

    (7/10)^2/2=49/200=Q.                            (7)

Equations (3),(5),(6) give one finite explicit cover of all three
entire candidate planes, every cap of mass at most Q. Therefore the
maximum depth of the finite three-fiber union is at most Q/M.

## 4. Matching lower bound and the strict target violation

Take the centroid of D at base1, namely (1,7/20,7/20). Every closed
ambient halfspace containing this point receives at least gamma_2 c
from D alone, by the ordinary continuous Grünbaum inequality in its
two-dimensional fiber. If the restriction of that halfspace to the
fiber is the whole plane, its contribution is c and the same bound
holds. It cannot be an empty restriction. Thus this is a genuine
point of the measured union with depth at least

    gamma_2 c/M=(4/9)(441/800)/(893/800)=196/893.

The explicit upper covers prove exact equality:

    max_depth=Q/M=196/893 < 2/9=gamma_2/h(P),        (8)

with exact gap 2/9-196/893=22/8037>0. The cited ordinary Grünbaum
inequality is only needed for equality in (8); the explicit upper
certificate by itself already disproves the finite-base target.

## 5. Why this is not a mixed-integer counterexample

The measured base is the specified finite set {0,1/100,1}. It is not
Z intersect the projection of C. Scaling the base by100 gives the
integer sites {0,1,100}, but convexity creates positive-area fibers at
EVERY integer between them. For instance, the section at integer2
contains the positive-area Minkowski combination of the fibers at1
and100 with base average2. Those extra fibers contribute to both total
mass and cap masses in OC and cannot be omitted.

More intrinsically, no affine identification of this three-point
collinear configuration with a complete intersection of a segment
and a one-dimensional lattice exists: three consecutive lattice points
in a segment have equal adjacent spacings, whereas these spacings
are in ratio1:99. Projective transformations preserve interval traces
and h(P) but do not preserve this completeness property.

This failure can occur along the projective orbit of a completely valid,
OC-safe lattice family. At integer bases0,1,2 take fibers198 A,100 B,2 D.
They are actual sections because99 A+D is contained in100 B, exactly
the inclusion (2) after scaling. Their projection is[0,2], so these
are all of their integer fibers. The middle fiber has area5000, whereas
the total area is1510093/200<10000; its own centroid therefore already
proves the OC target by the heavy-fiber argument.

The full projective transformation

    (z,x,y) -> (z,x,y)/(198-98z)

has positive denominator on this entire body's projection. It sends
the three integer bases0,1,2 to0,1/100,1 and their fibers exactly to
A,B,D. Thus preserving convexity, halfspaces, the number of sites, and
their Helly number under a projective map cannot preserve the claimed
UNWEIGHTED finite-base depth bound. The fiber Jacobian factors differ.
This is an explicit safe source and exact failing image, not just an
abstract objection that a normalization might change the lattice.

## 6. Consequences for the proof search

The unrestricted numerical statement beta>=gamma_d/h(P) for every
positive actual family on an arbitrary finite P must no longer be
treated as a plausible missing lemma: it is explicitly false.

The archived fixed-base attained-counterexample reduction and the
projective-orbit compactness theorem remain conditional geometric
statements. This example does not refute their proofs. In particular,
the projective-orbit theorem may produce a real below-target minimum
here: all one- and two-point bases satisfy their elementary targets.
Consequently no necessary projective-variation conditions, including
the new exact two-jet test, can force the false numerical target for
all finite bases. Likewise the general shape-minimum conditions cannot
imply that false target without extra information about the base.

The original OC task retains the arithmetic condition that EVERY
lattice point in the projection is present with its actual fiber.
Any successful use of the finite-base extremal route must preserve
and exploit that condition, or another proved consequence that excludes
this counterexample. Projective preservation of h(P) alone is insufficient.

There is a stronger implication for the archived variational approaches.
On this fixed three-point base the dependence space L(P) is just the
ordinary affine functions, so it is already canonical and connected.
Every proper closed minor has at most two points and satisfies its
gamma_2/h target by the heaviest-fiber centroid bound. Applying the
proved attained-counterexample reduction to (8) therefore supplies an
UNRESTRICTED all-positive minimum on this same affine three-site
configuration, strictly below gamma_2/2. The smaller-minor escape in
that reduction is impossible here. Thus even genuine local minimality,
all selected critical covers, and all their necessary boundary stresses
cannot force the unrestricted gamma_d/h(P) bound. This is not merely
another example satisfying one convenient incomplete stress system.

It also refutes the exploratory claim that every all-positive canonical
minimum has depth at least gamma_d/(dim aff(P)+1): here the base dimension
is1 and the attained minimum is below gamma_2/2. Restricting to a genuinely
lattice-complete base is essential for any possible repaired statement.
